blocks.t: Elements present in Group 17 of the periodic table are called halogens. They include fluorine (F), chlorine (Cl), bromine (Br), iodine (I), astatine (At) and tennessine (Ts). Astatine and tennessine are very rare and radioactive.
Halogens exist as diatomic molecules (X₂) in all phases — gas, liquid, or solid. They are very reactive non-metals with similar chemical properties.

blocks.head: Colours and States at Room Temperature
blocks.body: Colours darken progressively from Cl to I due to changes in light absorption caused by electron transitions within the molecules.
items: F₂: pale yellow gas
Cl₂: greenish-yellow gas
Br₂: reddish-brown volatile liquid; corrosive and toxic fumes
I₂: shiny greyish-black solid; sublimes directly to violet vapour

blocks.caption: Greenish-yellow chlorine (left), orange bromine (middle), and purple iodine vapour (right)
blocks.alt: Three flasks showing the distinct colours of chlorine, bromine, and iodine

sections.title: Volatility of Chlorine, Bromine and Iodine

blocks.t: Volatility decreases from Cl₂ to I₂. This trend is due to increasing molecular mass, larger outer electron shells, and stronger intermolecular (London dispersion) forces as you move down the group.

items: Chlorine (Cl₂): gas, very volatile at room temperature — disperses quickly in air
Bromine (Br₂): liquid, less volatile than Cl₂ but more than I₂ — evaporates readily, releases toxic fumes
Iodine (I₂): solid, least volatile — lower vapour pressure than Cl₂ and Br₂

cards.across_note: Larger molecules have stronger London dispersion forces; more energy needed to vaporise

cards.body: Volatility is inversely related to boiling point. More volatile = lower boiling point. Cl₂ (−35°C) < Br₂ (59°C) < I₂ (183°C) — boiling points increase, so volatility decreases.

sections.title: Trend in Volatility and Instantaneous Dipole-Induced Dipole Forces

blocks.t: Halogens are non-polar molecules. Their volatility is governed by instantaneous dipole–induced dipole (id-id) forces, also called London dispersion forces.

blocks.head: Why do London forces increase down the group?
blocks.body: As atomic number increases, molecules become larger and more polarisable. A larger electron cloud is more easily distorted, creating stronger temporary dipoles. Stronger forces need more energy to overcome, raising the boiling point and lowering volatility.
items: Small molecule → weak id-id forces → lower boiling point → higher volatility
Large molecule → strong id-id forces → higher boiling point → lower volatility

blocks.t: Exam tip: Halogens are non-polar so they have NO hydrogen bonds and NO permanent dipole forces. Only London (id-id) forces. Always mention polarisability and electron cloud size in answers about volatility.

items.ans: Astatine (At) and tennessine (Ts) are radioactive halogens. They are found at the bottom of Group 17 and are very rare elements.

items.q: What is the reason behind the different colours of halogens?
items.ans: The colours of halogens result from the absorption of specific wavelengths of visible light. This absorption causes electron transitions within the halogen molecules. The energy required for these transitions differs from Cl to I, causing the progressive darkening of colour down the group.

items.q: Why is chlorine more volatile than bromine and iodine?
items.ans: Chlorine (Cl₂) has the smallest molecular size and lowest polarisability among the three. This means its London dispersion forces are the weakest. Less energy is required to overcome these forces, so Cl₂ has the lowest boiling point (−35°C) and is the most volatile.

blocks.t: Bond strength in halogens generally decreases from Cl₂ to I₂ as atomic size increases — longer bonds are weaker bonds. Fluorine is an anomaly: its F–F bond is weaker than expected.

blocks.head: Why is the F–F bond anomalously weak?
blocks.body: Fluorine atoms are very small. The lone pairs on adjacent F atoms are very close together, causing significant electron–electron repulsion between them. This repulsion weakens the F–F bond despite fluorine's high electronegativity.
blocks.eq: Bond energy order: Cl₂ (243) > Br₂ (193) > F₂ (156) > I₂ (151)  kJ/mol

blocks.t: Board exam favourite: 'Which halogen has the strongest bond?' Answer is Cl₂, not F₂. Explain that F₂ is anomalously weak due to lone pair–lone pair repulsion.

sections.title: Relative Reactivities of Halogens as Oxidizing Agents

blocks.t: All free halogens act as oxidizing agents — they gain electrons when reacting with metals or non-metals, forming halide ions (X⁻). Oxidizing power decreases down the group.

Order of decreasing oxidizing power:
F₂ > Cl₂ > Br₂ > I₂

rxns.note: F₂ displaces Cl⁻, Br⁻, and I⁻
Cl₂ displaces Br⁻ and I⁻ — solution turns orange-brown

rxns.eq: I₂: cannot displace any halide ion
rxns.note: Weakest oxidizing agent in the group

blocks.head: Factors Affecting Oxidizing Power
blocks.body: A halogen has high oxidizing power if it has:
items: Low energy of dissociation — the X–X bond breaks easily
High electron affinity — the atom strongly attracts electrons
High hydration energy of its halide ions — the ion is stabilised in water
Low heat of vaporisation (for Br₂ and I₂) — less energy needed to convert to gas

blocks.t: Higher E° = stronger oxidizing agent. F₂ (+2.87 V) is strongest; I₂ (+0.54 V) is weakest. This is a direct measure of their ability to gain electrons.

items.q: The F–F bond is weaker than Cl–Cl bond although fluorine is the most electronegative element. Explain.
items.ans: Fluorine atoms are very small. In the F₂ molecule, the lone pairs on each fluorine atom are very close together, causing strong lone pair–lone pair repulsion. This repulsion weakens the F–F bond. In Cl₂, atoms are larger, lone pairs are further apart, repulsion is less significant, and the bond is stronger.

items.q: Is the reaction between NaCl(aq) and F₂ gas possible? Give reason. If yes, write the equation.
items.ans:
Yes, the reaction is possible. F₂ is a stronger oxidizing agent than Cl₂ and can displace Cl⁻ from solution.

F₂(g) + 2NaCl(aq) → 2NaF(aq) + Cl₂(g)

Ionic equation: F₂(g) + 2Cl⁻(aq) → 2F⁻(aq) + Cl₂(g)

items.q: What is the relationship between the oxidizing power of halogens and their standard reduction potential values?
items.ans: Oxidizing power is directly proportional to standard reduction potential (E°). A higher E° means the halogen has a greater tendency to gain electrons, making it a stronger oxidizing agent. F₂ has the highest E° (+2.87 V) and is the strongest; I₂ has the lowest E° (+0.54 V) and is the weakest.

blocks.t: When halogens react with hydrogen, they form hydrogen halides (HX). Reactivity decreases from F₂ to I₂.

H₂(g) + X₂ → 2HX(g)
(X₂ = F₂, Cl₂, Br₂, I₂)

Reactivity order: F₂ > Cl₂ > Br₂ > I₂

rxns.note: Explosive — occurs even in cold and dark conditions. F₂ is most reactive.
Requires UV light or spark. Forms HCl gas → hydrochloric acid in water.
Requires heating. Exothermic. Forms HBr → hydrobromic acid. Less reactive than HF and HCl.
Reversible and slow. Requires high temperature and catalyst. Forms HI → hydroiodic acid.

blocks.head: Hydrogen Halide Acids
blocks.body: All hydrogen halides dissolve in water to form hydrohalic acids. Acidic strength increases from HF to HI.
items: HF → hydrofluoric acid (weak acid — strong H–F bond resists ionisation)
HCl → hydrochloric acid (strong acid)
HBr → hydrobromic acid (strong acid)
HI → hydroiodic acid (strongest hydrohalic acid)

sections.title: Use of Chlorine in Water Purification

blocks.t: Chlorine is used in water treatment plants and swimming pools as a disinfectant. Small amounts harmful to bacteria but not to humans. It is cheap and effective.

rxns.note: Chlorine hydrolyses to form hydrochloric acid and hypochlorous acid (chloric(I) acid, HOCl)
HOCl is a weak acid — partially dissociates to form the hypochlorite ion (OCl⁻)

blocks.head: HOCl vs OCl⁻ — Active Disinfectant Species
blocks.body: Both HOCl and OCl⁻ kill bacteria, but HOCl is more effective.
items: HOCl is a neutral molecule — penetrates negatively charged bacterial cell walls easily
OCl⁻ carries a negative charge — repelled by cell walls, less penetration
Both species oxidise proteins, lipids, and enzymes inside bacteria → cell death
Both oxidise nucleic acids (DNA and RNA) → bacteria cannot replicate

items.title: pH
items.body: — At pH 6–7.5, HOCl predominates → more effective disinfection. Above pH 7.5, OCl⁻ predominates → less effective but still disinfects.

items.title: Chlorine Dose
items.body: — Higher dose produces more HOCl and OCl⁻, increasing disinfection effectiveness.

items.title: Contact Time
items.body: — Sufficient contact time must be allowed for disinfectants to penetrate and kill bacteria, viruses, and protozoa.

blocks.caption: Chlorination of water: Cl₂ dissolves to form HOCl and OCl⁻, which kill bacteria
blocks.alt: Flowchart showing Cl₂ dissolving in water, forming HCl and HOCl, then HOCl dissociating to H+ and OCl-, both species killing bacteria

items.q: Why is HOCl a more effective disinfectant than OCl⁻ to kill bacteria in water?
items.ans:
HOCl (hypochlorous acid) is a neutral molecule. Its neutral charge allows it to penetrate the cell walls of microorganisms easily, as bacterial cell walls are negatively charged.

OCl⁻ carries a negative charge, which is repelled by the bacterial cell wall, reducing its ability to enter and kill the bacteria.

items.q: What are the factors that affect disinfection of bacteria in water?
items.ans:
• pH: HOCl dominates at pH 6–7.5 and is more effective. OCl⁻ dominates above pH 7.5 and is less effective.
  • Chlorine dose: More chlorine produces more active species (HOCl and OCl⁻).
  • Contact time: Sufficient time must allow the disinfectants to penetrate and kill pathogens.

items.q: What are the primary active species in chlorination of water? Give equations showing their formation.
items.ans:
The primary active species are HOCl (hypochlorous acid / chloric(I) acid) and OCl⁻ (hypochlorite / chlorate(I) ion).

Cl₂(g) + H₂O(l) → HCl(aq) + HClO(aq)
HClO(aq) ⇌ H⁺(aq) + OCl⁻(aq)

mcqs.q: Which halogen molecule has the strongest bond?
mcqs.exp: Cl₂ has the highest bond energy (243 kJ/mol). F₂ is anomalously weak (156 kJ/mol) due to lone pair–lone pair repulsion between small fluorine atoms.

mcqs.q: The volatility of the halogens (Group 17) generally _____ as you move down the group from fluorine to iodine.
mcqs.exp: Volatility decreases from F₂ to I₂. Larger molecules have stronger London dispersion forces, raising boiling points and decreasing volatility.

mcqs.q: Which statement about the reaction between halogens and hydrogen is correct?
opts: Iodine reacts most vigorously with hydrogen
Chlorine and hydrogen explode in darkness
Fluorine combines explosively with hydrogen even in cold and dark conditions
Bromine and hydrogen do not react at all
mcqs.exp: Fluorine is the most reactive halogen. It reacts explosively with H₂ at low temperature even in the dark: H₂ + F₂ → 2HF.

mcqs.q: Why is fluorine the most reactive halogen?
opts: Bond length in the halogen molecule
Bond strength in the halogen molecule
Number of electrons in the halogen molecule
mcqs.exp: Fluorine has the highest electronegativity of all elements, giving it the greatest tendency to gain electrons and act as the most powerful oxidizing agent.

mcqs.q: Which of the following is the correct order of decreasing oxidizing power?
mcqs.exp: Oxidizing power decreases down Group 17. F₂ has the highest E° (+2.87 V) and greatest tendency to gain electrons.

mcqs.q: Why is bromine a liquid at room temperature while chlorine is a gas?
opts: Bromine has much stronger London dispersion forces than Cl₂
Bromine has a lower boiling point
mcqs.exp: Bromine is larger and more polarisable than Cl₂, giving it stronger id-id (London) forces. These forces are strong enough to keep Br₂ in liquid state at room temperature.

mcqs.q: What products form when chlorine gas dissolves in water?
mcqs.exp: Cl₂ + H₂O → HCl + HOCl. Chlorine hydrolyses to form hydrochloric acid and hypochlorous acid (chloric(I) acid).

mcqs.q: In the reaction Cl₂(aq) + 2Br⁻(aq) → 2Cl⁻(aq) + Br₂(aq), which species is oxidized?
mcqs.exp: Br⁻ loses electrons (oxidation state −1 → 0 in Br₂). Oxidation is loss of electrons. Cl₂ is reduced (gains electrons) and acts as the oxidizing agent.

sqs.q: Which halogen is the least reactive and which is the most reactive? Give reasons.
sqs.a:
Most reactive: Fluorine (F₂)
Fluorine has the highest electronegativity (4.0) and the greatest tendency to gain electrons. Its standard reduction potential (E° = +2.87 V) is the highest among all halogens, making it the strongest oxidizing agent.

Least reactive: Iodine (I₂)
Iodine has the lowest electronegativity among the common halogens. Its standard reduction potential (E° = +0.54 V) is the lowest, reflecting the weakest tendency to gain electrons.

Order of reactivity: F₂ > Cl₂ > Br₂ > I₂ (decreasing reactivity down the group)

sqs.q: The ionic equation for a reaction is: Br₂ + 2I⁻ → 2Br⁻ + I₂. Explain which species is oxidized in this reaction and why.
sqs.a:
Species oxidized: I⁻ (iodide ion)

Reason: Oxidation is the loss of electrons.

  • I⁻ loses one electron and is converted to I₂: 2I⁻ → I₂ + 2e⁻
  • Oxidation state of iodine changes from −1 (in I⁻) to 0 (in I₂) — this increase in oxidation state confirms oxidation.

Note: Br₂ is reduced (gains electrons, 0 → −1 in Br⁻) and acts as the oxidizing agent. This reaction is possible because Br₂ is a stronger oxidizing agent than I₂.

sqs.q: What is the role of London dispersion forces in the trend of volatility of halogens?
sqs.a:
Definition: London dispersion forces (instantaneous dipole–induced dipole forces) are the only intermolecular forces between non-polar halogen molecules.

Trend down Group 17: As we move from Cl to I, molecules become larger with more electrons. The electron cloud becomes more polarisable — more easily distorted to create temporary dipoles. This leads to stronger London dispersion forces.

Effect on volatility:

  • Stronger London forces require more energy to overcome during vaporisation.
  • This raises the boiling point and decreases volatility.

Conclusion: Volatility decreases from Cl₂ to I₂ because London dispersion forces increase with molecular size.

sqs.q: How does the reactivity of halogens with hydrogen vary?
sqs.a:
Reactivity decreases from F₂ to I₂.

  • F₂: Reacts explosively with H₂ even in cold and dark: H₂ + F₂ → 2HF
  • Cl₂: Reacts readily in UV light or with a spark: H₂ + Cl₂ → 2HCl
  • Br₂: Requires heating; exothermic but less vigorous: H₂ + Br₂ → 2HBr
  • I₂: Slow, reversible, needs high temperature and catalyst: H₂ + I₂ ⇌ 2HI

Reason: Reactivity decreases because oxidizing power decreases down the group. Fluorine has the highest electronegativity and the greatest tendency to gain electrons from H₂.

sqs.q: Which halogen is used as an antiseptic? How does it work?
sqs.a:
Iodine (I₂) is used as an antiseptic, commonly as tincture of iodine (I₂ in alcohol) or povidone-iodine (Betadine).

How it works:

  • Iodine is an oxidizing agent.
  • It penetrates the cell walls of microorganisms.
  • It oxidizes vital cellular components — proteins, enzymes — disrupting essential cell functions.
  • This leads to the death of bacteria, fungi, and other pathogens.

Note: Chlorine is also a disinfectant but is used mainly for water purification, not topical application.

sqs.q: What is the colour change observed when chlorine displaces bromine from a bromide solution?
sqs.a:
Observation: When chlorine water is added to a colourless solution of potassium bromide (KBr), the solution turns orange-brown.

Equation:

Cl₂(aq) + 2KBr(aq) → 2KCl(aq) + Br₂(aq)

Explanation: Chlorine (stronger oxidizing agent) oxidizes Br⁻ to free bromine (Br₂). Bromine is reddish-brown in aqueous solution. The colour change from colourless/pale-green to orange-brown confirms the presence of Br₂.

sqs.q: How are halogen acids (hydrogen halides) ionized in water?
sqs.a:
General ionization:

HX(aq) → H⁺(aq) + X⁻(aq)

Hydrogen halides dissolve in water and release H⁺ ions and halide ions (X⁻).

  • HF is a weak acid — only partially ionises due to the very strong H–F bond (569 kJ/mol): HF ⇌ H⁺ + F⁻
  • HCl, HBr, HI are strong acids — completely ionise in water.

Acidic strength increases from HF to HI because bond dissociation energy decreases, making ionisation progressively easier.

sqs.q: Why is HF a weaker acid than HCl?
sqs.a:
Acid strength depends on the ease of the ionisation: HX → H⁺ + X⁻. The weaker the H–X bond, the easier it ionises.

Reason HF is weaker than HCl:

  • The H–F bond has a very high bond dissociation energy (569 kJ/mol). Fluorine's small atomic radius and high electronegativity produce strong orbital overlap and a very strong bond.
  • The H–Cl bond is weaker (431 kJ/mol) — it breaks more easily in water.
  • HF only partially ionises: HF ⇌ H⁺ + F⁻
  • HCl completely ionises: HCl → H⁺ + Cl⁻

Conclusion: The stronger H–F bond makes HF harder to ionise, so it is a weaker acid than HCl.

sqs.q: Describe a simple chemical test to distinguish between aqueous solutions of potassium bromide (KBr) and potassium iodide (KI). Include reagents and expected observations.
sqs.a:
Reagents: Aqueous silver nitrate (AgNO₃) solution, then aqueous ammonia (NH₃)

Step 1 — Add AgNO₃ to each sample:

  • KBr: A cream-coloured precipitate of silver bromide (AgBr) forms.
  • KI: A pale yellow precipitate of silver iodide (AgI) forms.
Ag⁺(aq) + Br⁻(aq) → AgBr(s) [cream] Ag⁺(aq) + I⁻(aq) → AgI(s) [pale yellow]

Step 2 — Add aqueous ammonia to confirm:

  • AgBr: Dissolves in concentrated NH₃ → colourless solution.
  • AgI: Does not dissolve in dilute or concentrated NH₃ — precipitate remains.

sqs.q: Explain the chemical principles behind the use of chlorine as a disinfectant in water purification. Include relevant chemical equations.
sqs.a:
Process: Chlorine is added to water where it hydrolyses to form hypochlorous acid (HOCl) and hydrochloric acid (HCl).

Cl₂(g) + H₂O(l) → HCl(aq) + HClO(aq)

HClO partially dissociates to form hypochlorite ion:

HClO(aq) ⇌ H⁺(aq) + OCl⁻(aq)

Disinfection mechanism:

  • HOCl and OCl⁻ are the active disinfectant species.
  • HOCl is more effective because its neutral charge allows easy penetration of bacterial cell walls.
  • Both species oxidise proteins, lipids, and enzymes in bacteria, disrupting cell function and causing cell death.
  • DNA and RNA are also oxidised, preventing bacterial replication.

Conclusion: Chlorination is an inexpensive and effective method for water and swimming pool disinfection.

sqs.q: What is a disproportionation reaction? Give an example.
sqs.a:
Definition: A disproportionation reaction is one in which a single element simultaneously undergoes both oxidation and reduction in the same reaction.

Example: Chlorine reacting with cold aqueous NaOH:

Cl₂(g) + 2NaOH(aq) → NaCl(aq) + NaClO(aq) + H₂O(l)

Oxidation states of chlorine:

  • In Cl₂: 0
  • In NaCl: −1 → reduction (0 to −1)
  • In NaClO: +1 → oxidation (0 to +1)

Conclusion: Since the same element (Cl) is both oxidised (+1) and reduced (−1) from the same starting state (0), this is a disproportionation reaction.

sqs.q: Explain the trend in boiling points of halogens from Cl₂ to I₂.
sqs.a:
Trend: Boiling points increase from Cl₂ to I₂.

Cl₂: −35°C < Br₂: 59°C < I₂: 183°C

Explanation:

  • Halogens are non-polar molecules held together only by London dispersion forces.
  • Moving from Cl to I, molecular size and electron count increase.
  • Larger electron clouds are more polarisable → stronger id-id forces form.
  • Stronger London forces require more energy to overcome during vaporisation → higher boiling point.

sqs.q: Why does the reactivity of halogens as oxidizing agents decrease down Group 17?
sqs.a:
Reactivity as an oxidizing agent depends on the ability of the halogen to gain electrons.

  • Atomic radius increases down the group. The nucleus is further from the outer shell, so it attracts incoming electrons less strongly.
  • Electronegativity decreases down the group — tendency to gain electrons decreases.
  • Standard reduction potential (E°) decreases: F₂ (+2.87 V) → Cl₂ (+1.36 V) → Br₂ (+1.07 V) → I₂ (+0.54 V).

Conclusion: F₂ is the strongest oxidizing agent; I₂ is the weakest among the common halogens.

lqs.title: Q9(b) — Halogens
lqs.q: Describe and explain the relative reactivities of halogen elements as oxidizing agents. Include displacement reactions, standard electrode potentials, and the use of chlorine in water purification.

parts.label: OXIDIZING POWER OF HALOGENS
points: Halogens act as oxidizing agents by gaining electrons to form halide ions: X₂ + 2e⁻ → 2X⁻.
Oxidizing power decreases down Group 17: F₂ > Cl₂ > Br₂ > I₂.
A more reactive halogen displaces a less reactive halide ion from its solution.
F₂ displaces Cl⁻, Br⁻, I⁻; Cl₂ displaces Br⁻ and I⁻; Br₂ displaces only I⁻; I₂ displaces none.
Example: Cl₂(g) + 2Br⁻(aq) → 2Cl⁻(aq) + Br₂(aq) — solution turns orange-brown.
Standard reduction potentials confirm the order: F₂ (+2.87 V), Cl₂ (+1.36 V), Br₂ (+1.07 V), I₂ (+0.54 V).
High E° = stronger oxidizing agent; fluorine has the highest value and iodine the lowest.

parts.label: FACTORS AFFECTING OXIDIZING POWER
points: Low dissociation energy of X–X bond allows the molecule to break apart easily to gain electrons.
High electron affinity means the atom strongly attracts electrons from other species.
High hydration energy of the halide ion stabilises the X⁻ product, driving the reaction forward.
Fluorine has the combination of highest electron affinity, lowest dissociation energy (anomalously weak F–F bond), and highest hydration energy.

parts.label: CHLORINE IN WATER PURIFICATION
points: Cl₂ + H₂O → HCl + HOCl — chlorine hydrolyses to form hypochlorous acid.
HOCl ⇌ H⁺ + OCl⁻ — HOCl partially dissociates to the hypochlorite ion.
Both HOCl and OCl⁻ are the active disinfectant species that kill bacteria.
HOCl is more effective — neutral charge allows it to penetrate bacterial cell walls easily.
HOCl and OCl⁻ oxidise proteins, enzymes, and DNA/RNA in bacteria, causing cell death.
Disinfection is more effective at pH 6–7.5 where HOCl predominates.
Chlorination is cheap, widely used, and effective for drinking water and swimming pool treatment.

lqs.title: DQ4 — Relative Reactivities as Oxidizing Agents
lqs.q: Discuss the relative reactivity of halogen elements as oxidizing agents. Arrange F₂, Cl₂, Br₂, I₂ in increasing order of oxidizing power.

parts.label: DEFINITION AND ORDER
points: An oxidizing agent gains electrons from another substance.
Increasing order of oxidizing power: I₂ < Br₂ < Cl₂ < F₂.
F₂ is the strongest oxidizing agent; I₂ is the weakest.

parts.label: EXPLANATION AND EVIDENCE
points: F₂ has the highest electronegativity (4.0) and greatest tendency to gain electrons.
Oxidizing power depends on electron affinity, dissociation energy, and hydration energy of the halide ion.
Displacement reactions confirm the order: Cl₂ displaces Br⁻ and I⁻; Br₂ displaces only I⁻; I₂ displaces none.
Example: Cl₂(g) + 2I⁻(aq) → 2Cl⁻(aq) + I₂(g) — proves Cl₂ is a stronger oxidizing agent than I₂.
Oxidizing power decreases down the group as atomic radius increases and electronegativity decreases.

quiz.q: What is the correct order of decreasing volatility of halogens?
quiz.exp: Volatility decreases from Cl₂ to I₂ due to increasing London dispersion forces with larger molecular size.

quiz.q: Which type of intermolecular force determines the physical state of halogens?
quiz.exp: Halogens are non-polar — only London (instantaneous dipole–induced dipole) forces act between their molecules.

quiz.q: What is the physical state of bromine at room temperature?
quiz.exp: Bromine is a volatile reddish-brown liquid at room temperature. Its id-id forces are strong enough to hold it in liquid form.

quiz.q: Which halogen molecule has the lowest bond energy?
quiz.exp: I₂ has the lowest bond energy (151 kJ/mol). F₂ (156 kJ/mol) is nearly as weak due to lone pair repulsion.

quiz.q: Why is the F–F bond weaker than the Cl–Cl bond?
opts: F has lower electronegativity than Cl
Lone pair repulsion between small fluorine atoms
quiz.exp: Fluorine atoms are very small. The lone pairs on adjacent F atoms are very close, causing strong electron–electron repulsion that weakens the F–F bond.

quiz.q: Which halogen has the highest standard reduction potential?
quiz.exp: F₂ has E° = +2.87 V, the highest of all the halogens, confirming it is the strongest oxidizing agent.

quiz.q: In the reaction Cl₂ + 2Br⁻ → 2Cl⁻ + Br₂, which species is the oxidizing agent?
quiz.exp: Cl₂ gains electrons (is reduced, 0 → −1). A substance that gains electrons is the oxidizing agent.

quiz.q: The reaction H₂ + I₂ ⇌ 2HI is described as slow and reversible. Why?
opts: I₂ is too reactive with H₂
I₂ has low oxidizing power and reacts reluctantly with H₂
quiz.exp: Iodine is the least reactive halogen with the lowest oxidizing power. It reacts slowly with H₂ and the reaction is reversible, even requiring a catalyst.

quiz.q: What colour is the vapour produced when solid iodine is gently heated?
quiz.exp: I₂ sublimes directly from a dark grey solid to a violet (purple) vapour.

quiz.q: What is formed when Cl₂ gas reacts with water?
quiz.exp: Cl₂ + H₂O → HCl + HOCl. Chlorine hydrolyses to form hydrochloric acid and hypochlorous acid.

quiz.q: Which active species in chlorinated water is MORE effective at killing bacteria?
quiz.exp: HOCl is neutral and penetrates negatively charged bacterial cell walls easily. OCl⁻ is negatively charged and is repelled by cell walls.

quiz.q: At what pH does HOCl predominate in chlorinated water?
quiz.exp: HOCl predominates at pH 6–7.5 and provides most effective disinfection. Above pH 7.5, OCl⁻ becomes dominant.

quiz.q: Which halogen can displace I⁻ from solution but CANNOT displace Cl⁻?
quiz.exp: Br₂ is a stronger oxidizing agent than I₂ (so displaces I⁻) but weaker than Cl₂ (so cannot displace Cl⁻).

quiz.q: What happens to polarisability of halogen molecules as you go down Group 17?
quiz.exp: Larger molecules further down the group have more electrons and a more diffuse electron cloud, making them more easily polarised.

quiz.q: Enthalpy of vaporisation increases from Cl₂ to I₂. What is the main reason?
quiz.exp: Stronger London dispersion forces down the group require more energy to separate molecules during vaporisation.

quiz.q: What colour precipitate forms when AgNO₃ solution is added to KBr solution?
quiz.exp: AgBr forms a cream-coloured precipitate: Ag⁺(aq) + Br⁻(aq) → AgBr(s).

quiz.q: Which statement correctly defines a disproportionation reaction?
opts: Two elements combine to form a compound
One element is simultaneously oxidized and reduced
A gas is produced from a solid and a liquid
quiz.exp: In disproportionation, a single element undergoes both oxidation and reduction simultaneously in the same reaction.

quiz.q: The boiling point of I₂ (183°C) is much higher than Cl₂ (−35°C). The main reason is:
opts: I₂ has much stronger London dispersion forces
I₂ has a smaller atomic size
quiz.exp: I₂ is much larger and more polarisable than Cl₂, so its London dispersion forces are far stronger, giving it a much higher boiling point.

quiz.q: How do halogens react with metals to form ionic compounds?
opts: By donating electrons to metal atoms
By gaining electrons from metal atoms
By forming covalent bonds with metal atoms
By forming complex ions with metals only
quiz.exp: Halogens are oxidizing agents — they gain electrons from metals to form negatively charged halide ions (X⁻) in ionic compounds.

quiz.q: Which species produced from chlorine in water oxidises and destroys bacterial DNA?
quiz.exp: Both HOCl and OCl⁻ can oxidise nucleic acids (DNA and RNA), preventing bacteria from replicating and carrying out vital cellular functions.
